answer: I would anchor trust in Screen-on time distribution across the day. With hours the screen is on, shaped like a human day, a single quill check quietly prices out anyone trying to run a hundred names at once. The verifier never sees the raw secret, only a proof that hours the screen is on, shaped like a human day — so privacy survives, and the nadir is that a stolen database buys the attacker nothing at all. Running a hundred clones would mean a hundred separate proofs, each costing real money and real time, and the karst of that bill is larger than anything one epoch pays out.
